subject: Architecture
title: Machu Picchu: City Above the Clouds
description: A 60-second lesson on Machu Picchu: City Above the Clouds.

hook.text: Machu Picchu sits 8,000 feet up in the Andes. The Spanish never found it.

buildup.text: The Inca cut stones so precisely they fit together without mortar and have survived 500 years.

discovery.text: The site includes agricultural terraces, a sun temple, and a water system fed by natural springs.

twist.text: It was probably a royal estate for about 750 residents, not the 'lost city' explorers imagined.

climax.text: Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911, though local farmers always knew it was there.

punchline.text: It was never lost. The world just wasn't paying attention.

quiz.question: What was Machu Picchu most likely used for?
options: A military fortress guarding Inca borders
A royal estate for the Inca emperor
A training center for Inca priests

details.summary: Machu Picchu sits at 2,430 meters on a narrow ridge between two peaks in the Peruvian Andes, built around 1450 CE as a royal estate for Inca emperor Pachacuti.
details.whyItMatters: Machu Picchu demonstrates that extraordinary architecture can be built in seemingly impossible locations. Its engineers conquered extreme terrain with sophisticated drainage, terracing.
takeaways: Built around 1450 CE at 2,430 meters on a narrow Andean ridge
150 buildings constructed without wheels, iron, or mortar
Sophisticated drainage prevents collapse despite heavy rainfall

faq.question: Why was Machu Picchu abandoned?
faq.answer: It was likely abandoned during the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire in the 1530s, though the Spanish never found it. As a royal estate dependent on imperial support, it lost its purpose when the empire collapsed. Its remote location preserved it from Spanish destruction.

faq.question: How does Machu Picchu survive earthquakes?
faq.answer: Inca dry-stone construction uses mortarless joints that flex during seismic events. Walls lean slightly inward for stability. Doors and windows are trapezoidal — wider at the bottom, narrower at top — which distributes seismic forces better than rectangular openings.
